1.pericope_label: Now it came to pass, when the wall was built, and I had set up the doors, and the porters and the singers and the Levites were appointed, That I gave my brother Hanani, and Hananiah the ruler of the palace, charge over Jerusalem: for he was a faithful man, and feared God above many. And I said unto them, Let not the gates of Jerusalem be opened until the sun be hot; and while they stand by, let them shut the doors, and bar them: and appoint watches of the inhabitants of Jerusalem, every one in his watch, and every one to be over against his house. Now the city was large and great: but the people were few therein, and the houses were not builded.

schools.summary: Gill reads the gate order as a security measure timed to daylight, holding out until the heat of the day so that ambush would be visible and the townsmen awake and armed. On the closing verse he goes to the dimensions, noting that the wall followed its old foundation and so enclosed the original area, and setting two ancient estimates of the circuit against each other, one of about six miles and one a little under.

Henry takes the appointment of porters, singers and Levites as the revival of temple service rather than a watch roster, on the principle that worship is a city’s real defence and ministers are the watchmen on its walls; he allows the narrower sense as well, that they were being readied for the dedication. He treats the two governors as complementary appointments, the brother who first brought the news of the ruin and the palace officer promoted for proven faithfulness, and refers the commendation to the second. From the phrase about fearing God above many he draws the observation that among true fearers of God some are eminent, and are owed a double share of honour.

Clarke refers the commendation to Hanani and turns it into a specification for public office — belief in God’s government, devotion to the people’s interest, government by law, protection of religion, and freedom from oppression and bribery. On the gates he takes the order to mean simply that they open at sunrise and shut at sunset, illustrating it from a practice of eastern cities in his own day where late arrivals sleep outside the walls, and notes that each householder guarded the wall opposite his own door. Wesley reads the hour as broad daylight, when the townsmen would be ready for an assault, and both explain the appointments by Nehemiah’s impending return to the Persian court.

Keil frames the chapter within the book’s sequence — fortification, then repopulation, then reform, then the ordering of Levitical service — and restricts the charge given to the gatekeepers, singers and Levites to the watching of walls and gates, on the precedent of the doorkeepers’ ancient duty at the sanctuary. He translates the gate order as a single instruction covering both the locking and the citizen watch, and observes that its verb for closing occurs only here in Hebrew. On the closing verse he is precise: the city was broad measured either way from the centre, and the statement about houses means that building had not kept pace with the walls, not that the place stood empty.

debates: Whether the faithful man who feared God above many is Hanani or Hananiah.
How late the gates were to remain shut: until sunrise, until broad day, or until near noon.
Whether the charge given to the porters, singers and Levites is a watch duty or the revival of temple service.
Whether the houses were not builded means the city had no houses or too few for its size.
outliers: Clarke turns the description of the governor into a general specification for public office.
Clarke supports his reading of the gate order from a custom he had observed in eastern cities, where travellers arriving after dark must sleep outside.
Keil notes that the verb for barring the doors appears nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible.
Gill weighs two ancient measurements of the city’s circuit against each other rather than choosing one.
Clarke and Wesley independently explain the appointments by Nehemiah’s planned return to the Persian court.
themes: The wall built and the doors set up
Charge over Jerusalem given to two men
A faithful man who feared God above many
Let not the gates be opened until the sun be hot
The city large and great, the people few

5.pericope_label: And my God put into mine heart to gather together the nobles, and the rulers, and the people, that they might be reckoned by genealogy. And I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first, and found written therein, These are the children of the province, that went up out of the captivity, of those that had been carried away, whom Nebuchadnezzar the king of Babylon had carried away, and came again to Jerusalem and to Judah, every one unto his city; Who came with Zerubbabel, Jeshua, Nehemiah, Azariah, Raamiah, Nahamani, Mordecai, Bilshan, Mispereth, Bigvai, Nehum, Baanah. The number, I say, of the men of the people of Israel was this; The children of Parosh, two thousand an hundred seventy and two.

schools.summary: Gill reads the ascription to God as Nehemiah’s settled practice rather than a single acknowledgment. His main contribution is a mechanism for the numerical differences between this register and the earlier one: the first was compiled in Babylon from those who gave in their names to travel with Zerubbabel, this one after arrival, so that dropouts and deaths on the road reduce some figures while late joiners who had not registered increase others.

Henry explains why a census is a defence measure, since a city is held by the number and courage of its inhabitants rather than by its walls, and expands it into a policy about the balance between a capital and its country. On the discrepancies he argues by elimination, refusing the theory that the two lists are separated by forty years of growth, since households would have changed more in that time, and preferring copyists’ errors or divergent copies, while allowing the setting-out and arrival explanation as a third. He reads the register itself as keeping the families distinct until the Messiah, and as evidence of the notice God takes of his people by name.

Clarke traces Nehemiah’s dependence on God through purpose, action and expectation alike, and takes the register to be considerably older than Zerubbabel — a document that no longer matched the nation and that Nehemiah revised only in part, which is his account of why it differs from the earlier copy. He declines to annotate the list, since it is almost identical with the chapter that carries it already. Wesley’s note on the divine prompting reproduces Henry’s wording closely.

Keil identifies the resolution precisely — to convene the nobles and rulers so the people could be reckoned by genealogy, giving a basis for the repopulation just shown to be needed — and takes those who came up at the first to be the company under Cyrus with Zerubbabel and Jeshua rather than the later one with Ezra. He states flatly that the list which follows is identical with the earlier register.

debates: Whose register Nehemiah found: the company that returned under Cyrus, or an older list predating Zerubbabel.
Why the numbers here differ from those in the parallel register.
Whether the differences are textual or historical.
Why a genealogical census was the right answer to an underpopulated city.
outliers: Gill accounts for the discrepancies by the difference between a list of intended travellers and a list of actual arrivals.
Henry rejects the reading that the two lists are separated by forty years of natural increase, on the ground that the figures are too close for it.
Henry notes that the totals agree throughout except for the singers, where the two registers differ by forty-five.
Clarke leaves the list unannotated and refers the reader to the parallel chapter instead.
Wesley’s comment on the divine prompting is an abridgement of Henry’s rather than an independent judgment.
themes: My God put into mine heart
Reckoned by genealogy
The register of them which came up at the first
The children of the province
Differences from the earlier list

19.pericope_label: The children of Bigvai, two thousand threescore and seven.

schools.summary: Henry does not treat the verse individually, but his account of the register covers it: most figures agree exactly between the two chapters and a handful differ by one or two, which he puts down to the ordinary errors of transcription, numbers being especially liable to them.

Clarke notes a one-digit manuscript variant here, sixty-six for sixty-seven, and observes that the lower reading agrees with the parallel register. He reports it without deciding between the readings.

debates: Whether the number here or the lower figure in the parallel register is original.
outliers: Clarke reports the variant without choosing between the readings.
themes: The children of Bigvai
A one-digit manuscript variant

33.pericope_label: The men of the other Nebo, fifty and two. The children of the other Elam, a thousand two hundred fifty and four.

schools.summary: Clarke treats the two occurrences of the qualifying word separately. In the first he doubts the word belongs to the text at all, since the parallel register lacks it and many manuscripts here omit it, and he identifies the place with Nob or Nobah in Benjamin. In the second he finds the word necessary, since it marks this family off from an Elam entered earlier in the same list.

debates: Whether the word other belongs to the text in the first of these two lines.
Which place the register means by Nebo.
outliers: Clarke identifies the Nebo of this list with Nob, or Nobah, in the tribe of Benjamin.
The same word is textually doubtful in one line and functionally necessary in the next.
themes: The men of the other Nebo
The children of the other Elam
A doubtful qualifier

68.pericope_label: Their horses, seven hundred thirty and six: their mules, two hundred forty and five: Their camels, four hundred thirty and five: six thousand seven hundred and twenty asses. And some of the chief of the fathers gave unto the work. The Tirshatha gave to the treasure a thousand drams of gold, fifty basons, five hundred and thirty priests' garments. And some of the chief of the fathers gave to the treasure of the work twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand and two hundred pound of silver. And that which the rest of the people gave was twenty thousand drams of gold, and two thousand pound of silver, and threescore and seven priests' garments. So the priests, and the Levites, and the porters, and the singers, and some of the people, and the Nethinims, and all Israel, dwelt in their cities; and when the seventh month came, the children of Israel were in their cities.

schools.summary: Gill reads the giving plainly and keeps to what it was for: the fathers gave toward the building of city and temple, what went into the treasure funded the temple’s expenses and services, and he converts the people’s gold into the currency of his own day. On the closing verse he observes only that it repeats the earlier register.

Henry states the case against identifying this collection with the earlier one more strongly than anyone — the governor is absent there and opens the list here, and the single figure recorded there is larger than all the sums here combined — and still concludes that it is probably the same contribution reported from a different copy, because the two chapters close alike. He then declines to make the question load-bearing, on the ground that faith rests on the substance of law and gospel rather than on names and numbers, and adds that nothing given to God’s work is forgotten.

Clarke supplies the textual apparatus for the close of the register: the verse on the horses is missing from a large body of manuscripts and several versions, though the negative evidence of one of them is worthless because it omits the list entirely; a Vulgate sentence marking the end of the document has no ancient authority; and a Greek copy differs over the weight of silver and over whether the governor gave the gold or received it. He ends with the purpose of the whole exercise, that tracing families traced their ancestral towns, that the work took about a month between the completion of the wall and the settlement, and that a register left no ground for any charge of favouritism. Wesley identifies the Tirshatha as Nehemiah and treats the contribution as a separate one from the earlier collection.

debates: Whether the verse recording the horses belongs to the text.
Whether the Tirshatha gave the gold or received it for the treasury.
Whether this contribution is the same as the one in the earlier register or a separate collection.
Where the quoted document ends and Nehemiah’s own narrative resumes.
outliers: Clarke discounts one version’s omission of the verse because that version omits the entire list.
Clarke reports a Vulgate addition marking the end of the register and rejects it for want of any ancient support.
Henry argues against his own conclusion at length before accepting it, and then refuses to let the question carry any weight.
Clarke dates the whole operation to about a month, from the finishing of the wall to the people’s settlement in their cities.
Clarke reads the register as the guarantee of impartiality, since it decided the allocations and left no room for a charge against the governor.
themes: Horses, mules, camels and asses
The Tirshatha gave to the treasure
Gifts of the chief of the fathers
Differences from the earlier collection
All Israel dwelt in their cities
